videos.title: A framework for data analytics
videos.take: Data analytics starts with the business problem and ends with a deployed, monitored model

scenes.say: Management accountants now build prediction models, not just budgets. Here's the framework that keeps a model useful.

scenes.heading: Six steps
scenes.say: Six steps. Understand the business problem. Understand the data you have. Prepare it, cleaning errors and creating useful variables. Build a model. Evaluate it on data it hasn't seen. Then deploy it and keep monitoring.

sub: Which bike dealers will pay late?
scenes.say: Tallgrass sells through about two hundred bike dealers. Some pay months late, which costs Tallgrass about $3,000 per late account in financing, collection and write-offs. Ana wants to predict which dealers will pay late.

scenes.heading: Kinds of analytics
scenes.say: Descriptive analytics says what happened. Predictive analytics says what's likely to happen. Prescriptive analytics recommends what to do. Ana needs all three.

sub: A model is only worth building if
scenes.say: The first step is the most important: a model is worth building only if its predictions will change a decision, here whether to demand prepayment.

scenes.q: Splitting addresses into city and state and filling missing values is which step?
scenes.say: Quick check. Cleaning addresses and filling missing values is which step? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, data preparation, which often takes most of the time.

videos.title: Classification with decision trees
videos.take: A decision tree splits data on features to sort cases into classes such as late or on-time

scenes.say: Classification models sort cases into groups. The easiest to read is the decision tree.
A classification model predicts which category a case falls into. Here: will a dealer pay late, or on time? It learns from past dealers whose outcomes are known.

scenes.heading: Ana's tree
items: Yes, under 3 years a customer → late
Yes, 3+ years a customer → on time
scenes.say: Ana's tree first asks: was any payment more than sixty days late last year? If not, predict on time. If so, ask how long they've been a customer: under three years predicts late; three years or more predicts on time.

The variables the tree splits on are called features. Ana tried payment history, years as a customer, order size, region and a credit score. The tree picks the features that best separate late from on-time payers.
Trees are popular in accounting because managers can follow the logic and explain a decision to a dealer, unlike many black-box models.

scenes.q: A dealer had no payments over 60 days late last year. What does Ana's tree predict?
opts: It depends on years as a customer
scenes.say: Quick check. A dealer had no payments over sixty days late last year. What does the tree predict? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, on time. The 'no' branch ends there.

videos.title: Choosing splits: purity
videos.take: Trees choose the split that makes the resulting groups purest, measured by Gini impurity or entropy

scenes.say: How does a tree decide which question to ask first? It picks the split that makes the groups purest.

sub: 0 when a group is all one class;
scenes.say: One measure is Gini impurity: one minus the sum of the squared shares of each class. A group that's all late payers scores zero. A fifty-fifty mix scores point five, the worst for two classes.

scenes.heading: 40 dealers, 10 late
scenes.say: Start with forty dealers, ten of them late. The share late is a quarter. Gini impurity is one minus point two five squared minus point seven five squared: point three seven five.

scenes.heading: Split on 'over 60 days late last year'
scenes.say: Split on payment history. Twelve dealers were late last year, and eight of them pay late again: Gini point four four. Of the other twenty-eight, only two pay late: Gini point one three. Weighted, that's point two three, a big improvement on point three seven five.

scenes.big: Greedy, one split at a time
scenes.say: The algorithm tests every feature, takes the split with the biggest improvement, then repeats inside each branch.

scenes.q: Which group has the lowest Gini impurity?
scenes.say: Quick check. Which group has the lowest impurity? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Nine to one is the purest mix, with a Gini of point one eight.

videos.title: Overfitting and validation
videos.take: Test models on data they weren't built on; prune trees that fit noise

scenes.say: A model can be perfect on old data and useless on new data. That's overfitting, and validation catches it.

sub: Learning the noise in past data,
scenes.say: Overfitting happens when a model learns the quirks of its training data rather than the real pattern. Keep splitting a tree and eventually every leaf holds one dealer: perfect on past data, poor at predicting.

scenes.heading: Training and test data
scenes.say: So split the data. Build the model on a training set, say seventy percent of dealers. Measure its accuracy on the thirty percent it has never seen. Cross-validation repeats this with different splits.

scenes.heading: Ana's trees
scenes.say: Ana's two-level tree is eighty-six percent accurate on training data and eighty-four on test data. A five-level tree is a little better on both. A twelve-level tree is perfect on training data but only seventy-one percent on test data: overfitted.
Pruning removes branches that don't improve performance on new data. Simpler models usually generalize better.
Quick check. Which tree should Ana use? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Five levels has the best accuracy on test data.

videos.title: Evaluating predictions
videos.take: A confusion matrix shows true and false positives and negatives; accuracy alone can mislead

scenes.say: Ninety percent accurate sounds great. But accuracy alone can hide the mistakes that matter.

scenes.heading: Test set: 200 dealers, 30 actually late
rows: Flagged late, paid on time (false positive)
Not flagged, paid on time (true negative)
scenes.say: On two hundred test dealers, thirty actually paid late. The model flagged forty: twenty-four correctly and sixteen wrongly. It missed six late payers, and correctly cleared a hundred fifty-four.

scenes.heading: Three measures
scenes.say: Accuracy, the share of correct predictions, is eighty-nine percent. Precision, the share of flagged dealers who really were late, is sixty percent. Recall, the share of late dealers the model caught, is eighty percent.
Why not just use accuracy? Predicting that nobody pays late would be eighty-five percent accurate here, and completely useless.
And the two kinds of error cost different amounts. Missing a late payer costs about $3,000. Wrongly flagging a good dealer risks the relationship. That leads to the decision step.

scenes.q: A model flags 50 dealers; 35 are actually late, out of 40 late in total. What is recall?
scenes.say: Quick check. A model flags fifty dealers; thirty-five really are late, out of forty late in total. What's recall? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Recall is thirty-five out of forty: eighty-seven and a half percent.

videos.title: From prediction to decision
videos.take: Weigh the benefits of correct predictions against the cost of errors to decide whether and how to use a model

scenes.say: A prediction is only useful if it improves a decision. Ana must decide what to do with the dealers her model flags.

scenes.heading: The proposed policy
items: But a good dealer forced to prepay costs $800 of lost margin
scenes.say: The proposal: flagged dealers must prepay their orders. That avoids the $3,000 cost of each late payer caught. But a good dealer wrongly forced to prepay may buy less, costing about $800 of margin.

scenes.heading: Value of the model, per 200 dealers
scenes.say: Per two hundred dealers, catching twenty-four late payers saves $72,000. Wrongly flagging sixteen good dealers costs $12,800. The net benefit is $59,200, so the policy is worth adopting.

sub: Flag more: higher recall, more false positives
scenes.say: Ana can tune the model's threshold. Flagging more dealers catches more late payers but annoys more good ones. The best threshold maximizes net benefit, not accuracy.

scenes.heading: After deployment
items: Check for unfair treatment of groups
scenes.say: And after deployment, keep watching. Economic conditions change, models drift, and features can treat groups of customers unfairly. Monitoring is part of the job.

scenes.q: A new threshold flags 60 dealers: 28 true positives, 32 false positives. Net benefit at $3,000 and $800?
scenes.say: Quick check. A new threshold flags sixty dealers: twenty-eight true positives and thirty-two false positives. What's the net benefit? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's A. $84,000 saved minus $25,600 lost is $58,400, slightly worse than before.
